Field surveys of the pike characin Oligosarcus hepsetus in southeastern Brazilian coastal streams have provided insight into its early life history. At a stable water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the incubation period from fertilization to hatching lasts approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days]. The newly emerged prolarvae are minute, weighing only about 0.0005 grams [Wwb = about 0.0005 grams] at emergence, consistent with the small egg diameter of roughly 1 mm reported for this species. The yolk-sac fry absorb their endogenous reserves over the next few days, relying on this lecithotrophic phase before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The extended period of yolk dependency is typical for characids spawning in warm, productive waters, and the thermal regime of 27 °C accelerates developmental rates considerably. By the time of first feeding, the larvae have increased slightly in mass and begin to exhibit the characteristic pigmentation patterns of the genus.

As the juveniles of Oligosarcus hepsetus grow, they undergo a gradual morphological transformation from the planktonic larval stage into the streamlined piscivorous form of the adult. Sub-adults begin to show clear signs of reproductive maturation once they reach a standard length of 11.6 cm [Lp = 11.6 cm], which corresponds to a wet weight of approximately 13 grams [Wwp = approximately 13 grams] at the onset of puberty. This size at maturity is relatively modest compared to the maximum size the species can achieve, indicating that individuals reproduce well before reaching their asymptotic length. The onset of gonadal activity in males occurs with the initiation of spermiation, while females begin vitellogenesis, both processes being triggered by a combination of photoperiod and temperature cues typical of subtropical systems. Field records suggest that individuals attaining this size are usually between one and two years of age, depending on local productivity and food availability. Puberty thus represents a critical life history transition.

The reproductive output of the pike characin is notably high, reflecting its position as a fecund, iteroparous predator in neotropical stream ecosystems. Gravid females produce an average of 279 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 279 eggs per spawning event], and under the warm thermal conditions of their native habitat at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], they are capable of completing several spawning cycles annually. The annual frequency of reproductive events has been estimated at approximately 161 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 161 spawning events per year], yielding a substantial total fecundity over the course of a single breeding season. This high investment in offspring is characteristic of species that experience relatively high levels of egg and larval mortality in the planktonic phase. The relative fecundity of 161 eggs per gram of female body mass underscores the species' strategy of producing numerous small eggs rather than investing in large, well-provisioned oocytes. Such a tactic is common among characids inhabiting unpredictable hydrological regimes.

Adult Oligosarcus hepsetus can attain a considerable body size, with the largest individuals recorded reaching an ultimate standard length of 32 cm [Li = 32 cm]. The corresponding maximum wet weight for specimens of this length is approximately 279 grams [Wwi = approximately 279 grams], derived from length-weight relationships established for the species. This maximum body mass represents a nearly threefold increase over the mass at puberty, highlighting the substantial somatic growth that occurs after the onset of reproductive maturity. Such continued growth is typical of indeterminate growers, allowing older, larger females to contribute disproportionately more to the spawning stock through heightened fecundity. Large specimens are typically apex predators within their stream reaches, feeding predominantly on smaller fish and aquatic insects. The size structure of populations can vary locally depending on fishing pressure and habitat quality, but the species' capacity to exceed 30 cm in length places it among the larger characins in its genus.

Longevity data for Oligosarcus hepsetus, gathered from mark-recapture studies and validated by otolith annuli analysis, indicate that the maximum lifespan under natural conditions is approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years] when maintained at a mean annual water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This relatively short lifespan is consistent with a fast-paced life history strategy that balances high early fecundity against a modest total reproductive window. Individuals that survive the high mortality of the larval and early juvenile stages can expect to participate in at least three or four breeding seasons over their lifetime. The age at natural death is typically preceded by a period of reproductive senescence in the final year, during which spawning frequency and egg quality may decline. This life span places the species among the shorter-lived members of the family Characidae, a pattern often linked to the energetic demands of sustained reproduction in warm, productive environments. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest a similar longevity range.
